slides.notes: Deck 15 of the topic order. 32 terms. Tags: in the book text means a chapter uses and explains it; in the glossary means a glossary row; editor or docs means Epic's editor documentation or the editor itself (page named on the slide). Unreal was not run for the chapters; the meanings of Play In Editor and the Blueprint Editor parts come from knowledge of the editor because the Epic pages returned only navigation text.

slides.title: Perspective, orthographic, view modes and right-mouse fly
slides.source: Source: Epic documentation, “Unreal Editor Interface”, Viewport Toolbar and viewport controls.
slides.notes: Edge ratios and face greys are computed from a projected cube. The flight path integrates held keys at 100 px per second; the speed is illustrative.
slides.picture: A cube drawn in perspective and in orthographic projection with edge lengths measured. Then a cube drawn Lit, Unlit and Wireframe. Then a top-down room with a camera flying along a path while the right mouse button is held.

new_texts: Perspective shows depth; orthographic drops it, so parallel edges stay parallel.
Four edges are the same length in the cube. Perspective shrinks the far ones; orthographic keeps all four equal (1.00).
Perspective is the default view and works like a camera. Orthographic (Top, Front, Side) is for lining things up.
all_texts: Perspective shows depth; orthographic drops it, so parallel edges stay parallel.

new_texts: Ways to draw the same scene: Lit, Unlit, Wireframe and others.
Lit: light changes each face's grey (here from 120 to 240).
Unlit: every face is the same grey (226). Wireframe: edges only (12).
The scene did not change. Only how the viewport draws it.
View modes change how the viewport draws the scene, not the scene itself.

slides.title: Levels, and why .umap and .uasset cannot be diffed
slides.source: Source: Chapters 0, 1 and 5, “Doing the same thing in Unreal Engine”; glossary, Engine vocabulary.
slides.notes: Actor counts 12, 5 and 40 are illustrative; the sum is computed. The hex bytes are seeded. The binary quote is from Epic’s Perforce page as cited in Chapters 1, 4 and 5.
slides.picture: Step 1: three levels with eye toggles and a count of visible Actors. Step 2: a one-number change shows as a readable line in a text file but as Binary files differ for a .umap. Step 3: two people edit the same file; text merges both edits, binary keeps one.

new_texts: A level is one playable space, saved as a map file; the Levels window lists the levels in the world.
LEVELS WINDOW: EYE ON = LOADED IN THE VIEWPORT
12 + 5 + 40 = 57 with all three on; toggling Rooms off leaves 17.
The Persistent Level is the one that is always loaded.
The Levels window lists the levels in the world. Eyes switch them on and off in the editor.

new_texts: Binary asset and level files that a text tool cannot open or merge.
A reviewer can read one line in the text file and nothing in the binary one.
Epic says .uasset and .umap files are binary, so cannot be opened as text or merged in a text tool.

slides.title: Material Editor, Niagara and the Animation editors
slides.source: Source: Chapter 9 (Niagara); Chapter 10 (Notifies, Montages); Chapter 6 (Material Editor).
slides.notes: Colour = texture × brightness, per channel. Niagara particles are a seeded burst of 32 (Chapter 9 gives a burst count of 32). The 6-frame notify window follows the Chapter 10 sword example in shape only.
slides.picture: Step 1: a Material graph multiplies a texture colour by a brightness value and shows the result colour. Step 2: a Niagara emitter's module stack lights top to bottom and a burst of 32 particles flies. Step 3: an animation timeline with a playhead and a notify window that opens for six frames.

new_texts: A node graph that builds a material; its result node takes Base Color and more.
MATERIAL GRAPH: TEXTURE × BRIGHTNESS → BASE COLOR
Halve the Brightness scalar and every colour channel halves: the red channel goes 176 to 88.
all_texts: A node graph that builds a material; its result node takes Base Color and more.

slides.title: Collision: object type, response and preset
slides.source: Source: Chapter 4, “Doing the same thing in Unreal Engine”; Epic documentation, “Collision Overview”.
slides.notes: Rule: a pair gets the weaker of the two responses (Block over Overlap over Ignore); Chapter 4 states that both sides must agree.
slides.picture: A lane with a player, a pickup and a wall, and a table of each pair's two responses and the result. In step 2 the pickup's preset changes from OverlapAll to NoCollision and the result for the player and pickup pair changes to Ignore.

new_texts: Each object has a type, and a response to every other type: Block, Overlap or Ignore.
TWO RESPONSES PER PAIR; THE WEAKER ONE WINS
Block needs both sides to block. Overlap needs both sides to allow overlaps.
Each object answers Block, Overlap or Ignore for every other type. A pair gets the weaker answer.
all_texts: Each object has a type, and a response to every other type: Block, Overlap or Ignore.
TWO RESPONSES PER PAIR; THE WEAKER ONE WINS
Block needs both sides to block. Overlap needs both sides to allow overlaps.

new_texts: A named bundle of responses, such as BlockAll, OverlapAll or NoCollision.
Choosing NoCollision for the pickup sets all its responses to Ignore. Player–Pickup then reads Ignore.
all_texts: Each object has a type, and a response to every other type: Block, Overlap or Ignore.

slides.title: Before you trust an editor change
slides.picture: A checklist of six items drawn one at a time.

new_texts: Am I in the level editor, or in a running PIE window?
Did I change it while playing? Play changes are discarded.
Did I save the level and the changed assets?
Is this a Project Setting, or only my Editor Preference?
Is the file text, or .uasset and .umap that an agent cannot read?
Do both objects answer Block or Overlap for the pair?
Then say it exactly: not “try it”, but “press Play, then Stop, and read the Output Log”.
